analysis.title: FOMC Preview: Ghosting the CPI (for now)
key_insights: Natixis expects the Fed to hold the policy rate at an upper bound of 4.00% at Wednesday's meeting, one month after its first hike in three years. September CPI was hotter than comfortable but is not expected to prompt a hike.
Natixis expects another round of hawkish dissents in favor of a 25bp hike from the three July dissenters: Logan, Hammack and Kashkari.
Chair Warsh has said he looks at broader trends rather than single data points. A pause buys the Committee time to see whether September CPI was noise or a signal.
If the next few inflation reports do not cooperate, the September CPI print could come back to affect the December meeting, where Natixis still expects one final hike this cycle.

Williams and Jefferson, two-thirds of the Fed leadership troika, previewed a pause by saying there is no urgency to hike at consecutive meetings. Waller emphasized flexibility on timing. Markets have leaned on these comments as a signal of inaction.

Natixis thinks a surprise hike by Warsh is possible and would likely have enough FOMC support, but judges it unlikely. Yield volatility and shakiness in tech/AI names have reduced the urgency to tighten financial conditions further.
Natixis sees the political calendar (midterm elections, White House scrutiny) as another reason to avoid a surprise hike, though it does not think politics will drive the decision.

Press conference expectations: Warsh will likely say the Committee focuses on trends rather than any one data print, mention financial conditions as presenting two-sided risks, and hold a brief presser without follow-up questions. Natixis expects shorter, less informative pressers under Warsh.

Growth is disproportionately driven by AI-related investment and the wealth it created. Natixis says concern about the sustainability of that part of the economy is paramount and recent trends warrant caution.

Natixis is cautiously optimistic, with less confidence than before. If tariff and energy-cost pressures wane, domestically generated inflation should keep slowing and core inflation should trend down. Consumer confidence is low and real wage gains are flat to negative.

Natixis forecasts slower growth, which should contribute to disinflation and prompt Fed caution against overtightening. It forecasts just one more hike this cycle, in December, contingent on encouraging inflation data and growth concerns.

risk_factors: Further hotter-than-expected inflation reports could revive the September CPI as a driver of the December decision.
Warsh could push for a surprise hike at this meeting, which Natixis judges unlikely.
The sustainability of AI-related investment and the wealth it created is a risk to growth and market health.
Tariffs and higher energy costs are acyclical sources of price pressure that may not wane.
Low consumer confidence and flat to negative real wage gains weigh on demand.
vol_and_positioning: Natixis cites volatility in yields and some shakiness in tech/AI names in the intermeeting period as reducing the urgency to tighten financial conditions further.

Recent moves in credit spreads, mortgage rates, higher yields and volatility are noted. Natixis says a Warsh mention of financial conditions should be read as two-sided risk rather than dovish, so long as conditions do not loosen.
geopolitical: Midterm elections are approaching, and Natixis notes the Fed will be mindful of political scrutiny from the White House if it hikes.
Tariffs are cited as an acyclical driver of price pressures that Natixis assumes will wane.

tension_points.bull_case: A pause lets the Fed see whether September CPI was noise. Slower growth, low consumer confidence and flat to negative real wages should drive disinflation, leaving only one more hike in December.
tension_points.bear_case: Hawks (Logan, Hammack, Kashkari) want a 25bp hike now, and Logan sees 50bp or more needed. A hotter CPI trend could make December a live hike and Warsh could surprise with a hike.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A string of inflation reports that do not cooperate in the coming months would undermine the one-more-hike call.

theme_stances.key_argument: The Fed will pause in October because leadership previewed no urgency, then hike once more in December if inflation data cooperate.
theme_stances.evidence: we are forecasting just one more hike this cycle
